timeline.body: The CIA and MI6 overthrew Iran's democratically elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh after he nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, installing Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi as an authoritarian Western client — the original sin of US-Iran relations.

Under Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace program, the United States supplied Iran with its first nuclear reactor and enriched uranium, seeding the very nuclear capability it would spend decades trying to destroy.
Iran's Islamic Revolution overthrew the Shah, severed all ties with Israel, and handed the former Israeli embassy in Tehran to the Palestine Liberation Organization.
Iranian students stormed the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 American diplomats hostage for 444 days, freezing US-Iran relations into a state of permanent crisis that has never thawed.
Iraq invaded Iran with tacit American approval, beginning an eight-year war that killed roughly 500,000 people — the deadliest conventional war between developing nations in modern history.
Six Gulf monarchies founded the Gulf Cooperation Council largely in response to the Iranian Revolution, creating the regional security bloc now weighing whether to enter the current conflict.

Israeli jets destroyed Iraq's Osirak nuclear reactor near Baghdad in Operation Opera, establishing the Begin Doctrine: Israel would preventively strike any nuclear capability in the region and explicitly declared this policy permanent.
Hezbollah emerged in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley with Iranian funding and Revolutionary Guard training, becoming the template for Iran's network of proxy forces across the Middle East.
The Iran-Contra affair revealed the Reagan administration had secretly sold weapons to Iran — the same country it was publicly helping Iraq fight — and funneled the profits to Nicaraguan rebels.
The US Navy began escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers through the Strait of Hormuz during the Tanker War, establishing the first direct American military commitment to keeping the strait open.
USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 civilians aboard — the US government awarded the ship's captain a Legion of Merit and never formally apologized.

The US invasion of Iraq destroyed Iran's greatest regional rival and inadvertently empowered Shia political movements across the Middle East, dramatically expanding Iranian influence from Baghdad to Beirut.

Iran transmitted a secret proposal to Washington through the Swiss ambassador offering full nuclear transparency, cooperation against al-Qaeda, and acceptance of a two-state solution for Palestine — the Bush administration refused to even discuss it.

Iran, the US, and five other world powers signed the JCPOA nuclear deal, trading sanctions relief for strict limits on uranium enrichment and the most intrusive nuclear inspections regime ever negotiated.
President Trump unilaterally withdrew the US from the JCPOA and reimposed maximum-pressure sanctions, prompting Iran to resume enriching uranium far beyond the deal's limits.

A US drone strike killed Iranian General Qasem Soleimani at Baghdad airport — Iran retaliated by firing ballistic missiles at American bases in Iraq, the first direct Iranian military strike against US forces.
The Abraham Accords normalized relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco, reshaping the regional order into an emerging anti-Iran coalition backed by the United States.

The Strait of Hormuz narrows to just 24 miles between Iran and Oman — roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply passes through it daily, giving Iran a chokepoint that no amount of military force can widen.

iran-us-israel-war.label: Iran-US-Israel war: Gulf states weigh military entry, Hormuz blockade tightens

timeline.body: President Hayes signed the Posse Comitatus Act barring the federal military from enforcing domestic law — but the civilian agencies Congress would create 124 years later under DHS fall entirely outside its restrictions.

Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti issued two legal opinions establishing that federal agencies must cease operations when their funding lapses, turning congressional budget disputes into government-wide shutdowns for the first time in US history.

President Reagan fired 11,345 striking air traffic controllers and permanently banned them from federal service, establishing the precedent that essential federal workers who keep airports running serve entirely at the government's pleasure.

Speaker Newt Gingrich forced two government shutdowns totaling 26 days after President Clinton vetoed Republican budget proposals, furloughing 800,000 federal workers and normalizing the shutdown as a routine political weapon.

Before 9/11, airport security screening was performed by minimum-wage private contractors hired by airlines — the same system that allowed 19 hijackers to board four commercial flights carrying box cutters on September 11, 2001.

Congress passed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act within 69 days of 9/11, federalizing all airport security screening under the newly created Transportation Security Administration and its 55,000 federal screeners.

The Homeland Security Act merged 22 federal agencies into the Department of Homeland Security, placing TSA, ICE, Border Patrol, the Coast Guard, the Secret Service, and FEMA under a single cabinet secretary with sweeping domestic authority.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement began operations by fusing the enforcement arms of the old Immigration and Naturalization Service and US Customs Service, creating an agency with broader domestic powers than either predecessor and no institutional culture to restrain it.
A 16-day government shutdown over Affordable Care Act funding forced TSA screeners to work without pay as 'essential' employees while 800,000 other federal workers were sent home.

US Customs and Border Protection claims legal authority to stop, question, and search anyone within 100 miles of any US border or coastline — a zone encompassing roughly two-thirds of the American population and every major international airport in the country.

TSA screeners earn a median salary around $47,000 — among the lowest in federal law enforcement — and were excluded from the standard General Schedule federal pay system until a 2023 reclassification that Congress had resisted for two decades.

The longest government shutdown in US history stretched 35 days over border wall funding; TSA sickout rates tripled, security lines exceeded two hours at major hubs, and federal employees lined up at food banks to feed their families.

Congress passed the Government Employee Fair Treatment Act guaranteeing back pay after shutdowns, but the law still permits the government to force essential workers to report for duty indefinitely without a paycheck during the shutdown itself.

The Trump administration rescinded longstanding ICE policies designating courthouses, schools, hospitals, and churches as 'sensitive locations' where immigration enforcement was restricted, expanding operations into spaces previously considered off-limits — including domestic airport terminals.

tsa-ice-dhs-shutdown.label: TSA workers unpaid in second shutdown as ICE militarizes airports
